name: Fenrir
description: A monstrous wolf, child of Loki and Angrboða. Bound by the gods with Gleipnir, Fenrir is foretold to kill Odin at Ragnarök before Víðarr avenges him.
sources: Poetic Edda: Völuspá; Prose Edda: Gylfaginning

name: Cerberus
description: The formidable hound who guards the realm of the dead. His number of heads varies among ancient accounts; the three-headed depiction became especially familiar.

name: Ammit
description: A supernatural devourer associated with judgment of the dead, depicted with crocodile, lion, and hippopotamus features.

name: Kitsune
description: Foxes in Japanese traditions can be associated with transformation, uncanny intelligence, and encounters with humans. Their roles differ widely by tale and region.

name: Qilin
description: An auspicious creature linked to virtue and wise rule. Its appearance and meaning have developed across Chinese literary and artistic traditions.

name: Lernaean Hydra
description: A many-headed serpent of Lerna defeated by Heracles as one of his labors. Accounts vary in details of its heads and regenerative powers.

name: Jörmungandr
description: The enormous world-encircling serpent associated with Thor and Ragnarök, and counted among Loki’s children.
sources: Poetic Edda: Hymiskviða; Prose Edda: Gylfaginning

name: Kappa
description: A water-dwelling figure often portrayed with a dish-shaped hollow on its head; local accounts portray it as mischievous, dangerous, or occasionally helpful.

name: Apep
description: A serpent associated with disorder who opposes the sun god during the nightly journey of the solar bark.

name: Fenghuang
description: An auspicious mythical bird associated with harmony, virtue, and legitimate rule, not identical to the reborn phoenix of Greek traditions.

name: Minotaur
description: A bull-headed figure confined in the Cretan labyrinth and defeated by Theseus.

name: Chimera
description: A fire-breathing composite monster with lion, goat, and serpent features, slain by Bellerophon.

name: Pegasus
description: The winged horse connected with Medusa and the hero Bellerophon in Greek traditions.

name: Sleipnir
description: Odin’s extraordinary eight-legged horse, described in the Prose Edda as the offspring of Loki and Svaðilfari.

name: Níðhöggr
description: A dragon or serpent associated with the roots of Yggdrasil and the imagery of the dead in Old Norse poetry.

name: Bennu
description: A sacred bird associated with solar renewal and creation, linked in later comparisons to the Greek phoenix.

name: Sphinx
description: A composite guardian figure, often represented as a lion with a human head; Egyptian and Greek sphinx traditions differ.

name: Tengu
description: A varied class of supernatural beings connected with mountains, ascetics, and martial legends; portrayals range from birdlike to long-nosed.

name: Oni
description: Powerful supernatural beings whose depictions and moral roles vary across Buddhist, literary, and folk traditions.

name: Yuki-onna
description: A female snow-associated supernatural figure appearing in varied regional Japanese stories.
sources: Regional Japanese folklore; later literary retellings

name: Long
description: Chinese dragons are diverse powerful beings associated with water, weather, and auspicious authority; forms vary by era and tradition.

name: Bai Ze
description: A legendary knowledgeable beast associated with accounts of spirits and supernatural beings.

name: Taotie
description: A name associated with a striking face motif on ritual bronzes and later literary interpretations; its status as a distinct creature is debated.
sources: Bronze art history; later Chinese texts

name: Ratatoskr
description: A squirrel who travels up and down Yggdrasil, carrying words between the eagle above and Níðhöggr below.
sources: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál; Prose Edda: Gylfaginning

name: Fáfnir
description: A figure who becomes a dragon guarding treasure and is slain by Sigurðr in the heroic cycle.
